query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of copper (≈1–2 at.%) into (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will improve its mechanical integrity by promoting the formation of ductile, Cu‐rich grain boundary phases, thereby reducing cracking without significantly altering its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: A (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy that delivers a strong field-induced caloric effect but exhibits poor structural integrity with a tendency to crack under mechanical load.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with approximately 1–2 at.% copper during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under applied magnetic and/or pressure fields and within the temperature regime of the caloric phase transition, accompanied by mechanical loading regimes (compressive/tensile) similar to those used in prior caloric performance evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ductile Cu-rich phases at the grain boundaries, either as thin segregated films or as coherent nanoprecipitates.
generation.mechanism: The copper dopant segregates to the grain boundaries, enhancing intergranular cohesion and impeding crack initiation and propagation, while the small volume fraction ensures that the underlying phase responsible for the caloric effect remains largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the copper-doped version is expected to exhibit significantly enhanced mechanical integrity (e.g., increased compressive strength and reduced crack propagation) while retaining a caloric response that is comparable (within roughly ±10%) to that of the baseline.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows a large caloric effect but suffers from cracking and limited mechanical strength under load.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under operating conditions typical of the caloric phase transformation (i.e., applied field, pressure, and temperature ranges that do not push the alloy beyond its designed phase stability) and when the copper addition remains low (around 1–2 at.%) to avoid altering the intrinsic phase transformation kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: While the directional improvements in mechanical properties are anticipated, the precise magnitude of strength enhancement and the acceptable threshold for caloric response retention require optimization and may vary with processing details.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples with 0%, 1%, and 2% copper doping under identical processing conditions. Confirm via microstructural characterization (using TEM and EDS) that copper segregates to grain boundaries. Subject all samples to identical applied magnetic/pressure fields and temperature conditions during mechanical testing (e.g., compressive and tensile tests) and measure the caloric response using metrics such as the isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature shift.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and morphology (via TEM/EDS)
Compressive strength, ductility, and crack propagation behavior (via standard mechanical tests)
Caloric response magnitude (entropy change or adiabatic temperature change under applied fields)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., less than a 50% increase in compressive strength or no detectable reduction in crack formation) or if the caloric effect is reduced by more than approximately 10% compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small addition of a ductile metallic element (such as 1–2 at.% copper) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will promote grain boundary segregation that toughens the microstructure, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity (e.g., increased compressive strength and reduced crack propagation) without significantly diminishing its large caloric response under applied fields.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that displays a large field‑induced caloric effect but suffers from poor integrity and cracking under operating conditions.
drafts.intervention: Doping the alloy with a small amount (around 1–2 at.%) of copper during synthesis, so that copper preferentially segregates at grain boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Tests conducted under operating conditions relevant for caloric effects – including applied magnetic or pressure fields and within the temperature regime where the phase transformation occurs – while subjecting the material to compressive and tensile mechanical loads.
drafts.structural_mediator: Copper atoms that segregate to and form a thin, ductile intergranular phase along grain boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The copper doping is expected to improve intergranular cohesion by acting as a ductile ‘glue’ that blunts crack initiation and propagation. Since only a minor volume fraction is added, the bulk phase responsible for the caloric effect is largely unaltered, preserving the large caloric response while improving mechanical robustness.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped alloy, the copper-doped alloy should show a significant increase in compressive strength (e.g., an enhancement by roughly 50% or more) and reduced cracking under load, while the caloric response (e.g., entropy change or adiabatic temperature change under field) remains at least comparable to that of the original alloy.
drafts.baseline: The unchanged (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with high caloric performance but limited mechanical integrity (evidenced by cracking and low compressive strength).
drafts.boundary: The proposed benefits are expected under applied-field and pressure-field conditions within the temperature window of the caloric phase transformation, and for mechanical testing regimes similar to those used in prior studies on analogous alloys. The minor copper addition must not exceed the level that could alter the transformation kinetics or the electronic/thermodynamic drivers of the caloric effect.

Characterize the microstructure (using TEM/EDS) to confirm copper segregation at grain boundaries. Perform mechanical tests (compressive and bending) and measure the caloric response under identical applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and interfacial structure (via TEM/EDS)
Compressive strength and toughness (using standard mechanical testing)
Magnitude of the caloric response (e.g., entropy change or adiabatic temperature change measurements under applied fields)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of copper does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., less than a 50% increase in compressive strength) or if it results in a measurable reduction in the caloric effect compared to the undoped alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of ductile Cu during synthesis—such that Cu-rich coherent nano-precipitates form at grain boundaries—will reinforce the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, improving its mechanical integrity against cracking while preserving its large caloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: The base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits a strong caloric effect under applied-field/pressure-field conditions but suffers from brittle behavior and low compressive strength.
drafts.intervention: Add 2–5 wt% Cu during alloy processing to promote in situ formation of ductile, coherent Cu-rich nanoprecipitates at grain boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Under applied magnetic field and/or pressure and at temperatures near the caloric phase transition; mechanical loading (especially compressive) regimes similar to prior tests.
drafts.structural_mediator: Coherent Cu-rich nanoprecipitates that refine the grain structure and toughen grain boundaries against crack propagation.
drafts.mechanism: The ductile Cu phase absorbs strain and bridges cracks at the microstructural level without significantly altering the transformation responsible for the caloric effect, thereby maintaining the caloric response while boosting mechanical integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: A revised alloy showing increased compressive strength (targeting improvements beyond previously reported ranges for epoxy-containing samples, e.g., >152 MPa), enhanced fracture toughness, and a caloric response within approximately 10% of the baseline alloy.
drafts.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with high caloric performance but poor mechanical integrity due to its brittle nature.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies under processing and operational conditions representative of the caloric transition region, with applied field, pressure, and temperature cycling regimes similar to those reported in prior studies. Its validity under extreme loading scenarios beyond those conditions remains unverified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize three sets of samples: one with 0 wt% Cu (control), one with 2 wt% Cu, and one with 5 wt% Cu added to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy. Process all samples under identical conditions. Subject the samples to calibrated applied magnetic field and pressure-field cycles near the caloric transition temperature while performing compressive strength and fracture toughness tests, alongside microstructural analysis to verify Cu-rich precipitate formation.
measurements: Caloric effect magnitude (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or entropy change)
Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM analysis for precipitate distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-containing samples show either (a) a reduction in the caloric effect exceeding a 10% decrease relative to the control sample, or (b) no statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., compressive strength and fracture toughness remain comparable to or less than the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A small microalloying addition of a ductility‐promoting element (e.g., 2–5 at.% Cu, substituted isovalently for one of the base elements) will promote a dual‐phase microstructure in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with refined grains and ductile grain‐boundary films that improve macroscopic integrity (crack‐resistance) without significantly altering the intrinsic caloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting high caloric response but poor integrity with a tendency to crack.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a minor amount (~2–5 at.%) of Cu during alloy synthesis, replacing a fraction of one or more constituent elements to foster a dual-phase microstructure.
drafts.conditions: Test under the same applied-field and pressure-field operating conditions (including similar temperature, magnetic field, pressure and loading regimes) as the base alloy to ensure that any changes in mechanical integrity and caloric response are attributable to the compositional modification.
drafts.structural_mediator: Refined grain size with the formation of a ductile, Cu-enriched grain-boundary phase (or nanophase) that spreads and redistributes stresses to impede crack initiation and propagation.
drafts.mechanism: The Cu addition is expected to segregate to grain boundaries and promote a slight phase separation that leads to a dual-phase (or gradient) microstructure. This microstructure enhances mechanical toughness and compressive strain capability via grain-boundary strengthening and improved ductility, while the overall entropy-driven caloric mechanism (e.g., magnetostructural or pressure-induced phase transformation) remains largely unchanged.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit significantly enhanced integrity (i.e., higher compressive strain to failure and reduced cracking under mechanical loads) with an estimated improvement on the order of 20–30% in ductility or strain tolerance, while retaining a caloric response within roughly ±10% of the original performance.
drafts.baseline: The current (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows a high caloric performance but suffers from poor structural integrity and cracking under operational conditions.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective when the Cu content remains low enough not to alter the essential caloric phase transformation characteristics. It is assumed that the operational conditions (applied field, pressure and temperature range) remain similar to those originally reported; deviations far outside these conditions may lead to unforeseen phase changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one using the standard composition and one modified with 2–5 at.% Cu substitution. Process both alloys identically. Characterize the microstructure (grain size, phase distribution, and segregation via electron microscopy and atom probe tomography), and then subject samples to compressive and tensile testing as well as caloric measurements (under applied magnetic/pressure fields) within the operational temperature and field ranges.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of compressive yield strength and plastic strain (ductility) via mechanical testing.
Microstructural characterization (grain size, phase distribution, Cu segregation) using SEM/TEM and atom probe.
Measurement of caloric response (e.g., entropy change, temperature change) under applied fields.
Comparison of crack propagation behavior (e.g., via digital image correlation or in situ mechanical testing).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g. >15% increase) in integrity (higher ductility and reduced cracking) while maintaining a caloric response within approximately ±10% of the standard alloy’s response, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a very small amount of boron (on the order of 0.1–0.5 at.%) during alloy synthesis will improve the mechanical integrity of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy through enhanced grain‐boundary cohesion, thereby reducing cracking without adversely affecting its caloric response.
drafts.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits excellent caloric response under applied-field/pressure-field conditions but suffers from poor structural integrity and a tendency to crack.
drafts.intervention: Introduce trace boron into the alloy system during melting/synthesis.
drafts.conditions: Tested under the same applied magnetic, pressure, temperature, and mechanical loading regimes used to measure its caloric performance (e.g., room temperature to moderately elevated temperatures under field cycling).
drafts.structural_mediator: Boron is expected to segregate to grain boundaries or form nanoscale boride clusters that reinforce intergranular bonding.
drafts.mechanism: By segregating at grain boundaries, boron improves cohesion between grains, reducing the initiation and propagation of cracks without significantly altering the phase transitions that drive the caloric effect.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy should exhibit higher fracture toughness and improved compressive/tensile integrity (i.e., reduced cracking) while retaining a caloric response of similar magnitude to that of the undoped alloy.
drafts.baseline: The undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large caloric response but poor structural integrity under load.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected when boron levels are maintained below approximately 0.5 at.%; higher levels might lead to the formation of brittle boride phases, and the improvement should be verified under the typical field/pressure and temperature regimes where the caloric effect is operative.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples, one undoped and one doped with ~0.2 at.% boron during synthesis. Process both identically, then subject them to compressive and tensile testing along with field-induced caloric response measurements under identical temperature, field, and pressure conditions.
measurements: Fracture toughness / crack propagation behavior (e.g., via microstructural analysis and mechanical tests)
Magnitude of the caloric response (e.g., isothermal entropy change or adiabatic temperature change)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (reduced cracking, higher fracture toughness) while maintaining an equivalent caloric response compared with the undoped alloy, the hypothesis would be falsified.
